newsitem.title: TAIWAN: United Micro plans T$500b wafer project.
newsitem.headline: United Micro plans T$500b wafer project.

text.p: Taiwan's United Microelectronics on Thursday announced a mammoth 10-year T$500 billion ($18 billion) wafer fabrication project, upping the stakes in the island's intense custom microchip war.

While analysts cautioned against oversupply as the company vowed to churn out more than one million wafers per month by 2007, they said surging global sales of personal computers likely would produce a subsequent rise in wafer demand.

The project, Taiwan's single biggest investment scheme to date, called for the completion of six advanced eight-inch and 12-inch fabrication plants in the island's burgeoning southern science park over a 10-year span.
"Given how bright the semiconductor industry's future is expected to be, UMC's investment is very normal and not extravagant," said Lin Yung-huei, research analyst for National Securities.
"The biggest demand for wafers will continue to come from personal computers," he said.
Industry experts forecast that the global integrated circuit industry would grow by an average of 15 percent per year for the next 15 years.
Such a rise would give Taiwan, which currently accounts for about four percent of global semiconductor output, plenty of room to stretch.

"Taiwan's electronics industry already accounts for some 30 percent of Taiwan's total manufacturing industry, and the ratio will soon raise to some 40 percent," said Alex Chen, research manager of HSBC James Capel in Taipei.
"It will become the main industry that supports Taiwan's future economic growth," Chen said.
United Microelectronics was not the only chipmaker that planned to pour prodigious resources into wafer fabrication.

In April their chief domestic rival, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, said it would launch a T$400 billion wafer project in the same science park that would host United Microelectronics' project.
Both projects, once completed, will dwarf Taiwan's most ambitious investment project to date -- a US$9 billion petrochemical plant being built in central Taiwan by Formosa Plastics group.
The first of United Microelectronics' six plants, budgeted at T$55 billion, is scheduled to go on line in 1999 with a capacity to produce 50,000 eight-inch wafers a month.

Once that project is running, United Micro plans to build five more wafer fabrication plants that will be designed to make more advanced wafers measuring 12 inches or more at a rate of 20,000 wafers a month.

The wafer fabrication complex will produce what the company called "special application" microprocessors and other chips, a signal that United Microelectronics is wooing the same custom-order foundry business that rival Taiwan Semiconductor has targeted.
United Microelectronics chairman Robert Tsao said he believed the huge investment carried little risk because global demand for advanced semiconductors continues to grow.
Analysts, however, said United Microelectronics and other chipmakers may have to join forces to upgrade their wafer production to the 12-inch phase due to a drastically higher cost of development.
"So far, no country in the world has built 12-inch wafer plants. To ensure success, Taiwan might need to find some U.S. partners to build the plants," said Ben Lee, analyst for Nomura Securities.
Tsao said United Microelectronics, which currently have three joint venture wafer plants in Taiwan, would consider forming more alliances in the future.
"That is obviously something we are open to, given the resources needed for development," he told reporters. ($ = 27.91 Taiwan Dollars)
